questions.stem_md: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 52^\circ$. The bisector of $\angle B$ meets $AC$ at $D$. Find $\angle ABC$, $\angle DBC$ and $\angle BDC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$AB = AC$, so $\angle ABC = \angle ACB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 52^\circ}{2} = 64^\circ$.

$BD$ bisects $\angle B$: $\angle DBC = \dfrac{64^\circ}{2} = 32^\circ$.

In $\triangle BDC$: $\angle BDC = 180^\circ - 64^\circ - 32^\circ = 84^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: Base angles $64^\circ$, half of that is $32^\circ$, and the angle sum in $\triangle BDC$ gives $84^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: The sides of a triangle are $6$ cm, $10$ cm and $(2x - 3)$ cm. Find the range of values of $x$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The third side lies between the difference and the sum of the other two: $10 - 6 < 2x - 3 < 10 + 6$, that is $4 < 2x - 3 < 16$.

Add $3$: $7 < 2x < 19$.

Divide by $2$: $3.5 < x < 9.5$.

questions.solution_md: Use $10 - 6 < 2x - 3 < 10 + 6$ and solve the double inequality to get $3.5 < x < 9.5$.

questions.stem_md: $ABCD$ is a quadrilateral. Prove that $AB + BC + CD > DA$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Join $AC$. In $\triangle ABC$ the sum of two sides is greater than the third: $AB + BC > AC$.

In $\triangle ACD$: $AC + CD > DA$.

Adding the two inequalities: $AB + BC + AC + CD > AC + DA$, and cancelling $AC$ gives $AB + BC + CD > DA$.

questions.solution_md: The diagonal $AC$ splits the quadrilateral into two triangles; the triangle inequality in each, added, gives the result.

marking_scheme.step: AB + BC > AC in triangle ABC
AC + CD > DA in triangle ACD

questions.stem_md: The angles of $\triangle ABC$ are $\angle A = (2x + 10)^\circ$, $\angle B = (3x - 5)^\circ$ and $\angle C = (x + 25)^\circ$. Find $x$ and arrange the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ in ascending order of length.

answer.model_answer_md:
Angle sum: $(2x + 10) + (3x - 5) + (x + 25) = 180 \Rightarrow 6x + 30 = 180 \Rightarrow x = 25$.

$\angle A = 2 \times 25 + 10 = 60^\circ$, $\angle B = 3 \times 25 - 5 = 70^\circ$ and $\angle C = 25 + 25 = 50^\circ$, so $\angle C < \angle A < \angle B$.

The side opposite the smaller angle is shorter: $AB$ (opposite $C$) $< BC$ (opposite $A$) $< CA$ (opposite $B$).

questions.solution_md: $x = 25$ gives angles $60^\circ$, $70^\circ$, $50^\circ$; order the sides by the angles opposite them.

questions.stem_md: $PM$ is the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $l$, with $PM = 20$ m. $A$ and $B$ are points of $l$ on the same side of $M$, with $MA = 15$ m and $MB = 21$ m. Show that $PA < PB$ without measuring.

answer.model_answer_md:
$A$ lies between $M$ and $B$ ($15 < 21$). $\angle PAB$ is an exterior angle of the right-angled $\triangle PMA$, so $\angle PAB > 90^\circ$.

In $\triangle PAB$ the angle at $A$ is obtuse, so it is greater than $\angle PBA$.

The greater angle is opposite the greater side, so $PB > PA$. (Check: $PA = 25$ m and $PB = 29$ m.)

questions.solution_md: The angle at $A$ is obtuse, so it is the largest angle of $\triangle PAB$ and the side opposite it, $PB$, is the longest: $PB > PA$, in fact $29 > 25$.

marking_scheme.step: angle PAB is exterior, so obtuse
angle A greater than angle B in triangle PAB
greater angle opposite greater side: PB > PA

questions.stem_md:
$ABCD$ is a kite-shaped frame with $AB = AD = 10$ cm and $CB = CD = 17$ cm. The bars $AC$ and $BD$ cross at $M$, and $BD = 16$ cm.

(a) Prove that $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC$.

(b) Hence prove that $\angle ABC = \angle ADC$ and that $AC$ bisects $\angle BAD$.

(c) Prove that $BM = MD$ and $\angle AMB = 90^\circ$, and find $BM$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$: $AB = AD$ (given), $CB = CD$ (given), $AC = AC$ (common). So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC$ by SSS.

**(b)** By CPCT, $\angle ABC = \angle ADC$, and $\angle BAC = \angle DAC$. Since $C$ lies inside the angle, $AC$ bisects $\angle BAD$.

**(c)** In $\triangle ABM$ and $\triangle ADM$: $AB = AD$, $\angle BAM = \angle DAM$ (part (b)) and $AM = AM$, so $\triangle ABM \cong \triangle ADM$ by SAS. Hence $BM = MD$ and $\angle AMB = \angle AMD$.

These two angles are on the straight line $BMD$, so they add up to $180^\circ$: each is $90^\circ$. Since $BM = MD$ and $BD = 16$ cm, $BM = \dfrac{16}{2} = 8$ cm.

questions.solution_md: SSS for the two halves of the kite, CPCT for the angles, then SAS for the triangles on either side of $AM$; the diagonals meet at right angles and $AC$ bisects $BD$, so $BM = 8$ cm.

marking_scheme.step: (a) the three equal pairs with reasons (given, given, common)
(b) angle ABC = angle ADC by CPCT
(b) angle BAC = angle DAC, so AC bisects angle BAD
(c) triangles ABM and ADM congruent by SAS
(c) angles AMB and AMD equal and add to 180, so 90 degrees

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $M$ is the mid-point of $BC$. The perpendiculars $ME$ to $AB$ and $MF$ to $AC$ are equal.

(a) Prove that $\triangle BEM \cong \triangle CFM$.

(b) Hence prove that $AB = AC$.

(c) If $\angle A = 50^\circ$, find $\angle B$, $\angle BME$ and $\angle EMF$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** In $\triangle BEM$ and $\triangle CFM$: $\angle BEM = \angle CFM = 90^\circ$, hypotenuse $BM = CM$ ($M$ is the mid-point of $BC$) and $ME = MF$ (given). So $\triangle BEM \cong \triangle CFM$ by RHS.

**(b)** By CPCT, $\angle B = \angle C$. The sides opposite equal angles are equal, so $AB = AC$.

**(c)** $AB = AC$, so $\angle B = \angle C = \dfrac{180^\circ - 50^\circ}{2} = 65^\circ$.

In $\triangle BEM$: $\angle BME = 90^\circ - 65^\circ = 25^\circ$, and by part (a) $\angle CMF = 25^\circ$ too. On the line $BMC$: $\angle EMF = 180^\circ - 25^\circ - 25^\circ = 130^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: RHS gives $\triangle BEM \cong \triangle CFM$, hence $\angle B = \angle C$ and $AB = AC$. With $\angle A = 50^\circ$: $\angle B = 65^\circ$, $\angle BME = 25^\circ$ and $\angle EMF = 130^\circ$.

marking_scheme.step: (a) right angles equal, hypotenuses BM = CM, ME = MF
(b) angle B = angle C by CPCT
(b) converse of the isosceles theorem: AB = AC

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 44^\circ$. A point $D$ on $AC$ is joined to $B$ so that $BD = BC$.

(a) Find $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ACB$.

(b) Find $\angle BDC$ and $\angle DBC$.

(c) Find $\angle ABD$ and $\angle ADB$, and name the longest side of $\triangle ABD$ with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $AB = AC$, so $\angle ABC = \angle ACB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 44^\circ}{2} = 68^\circ$.

**(b)** $BD = BC$, so $\angle BDC = \angle BCD = 68^\circ$ (angles opposite equal sides). In $\triangle BDC$: $\angle DBC = 180^\circ - 68^\circ - 68^\circ = 44^\circ$.

**(c)** $\angle ABD = \angle ABC - \angle DBC = 68^\circ - 44^\circ = 24^\circ$. $\angle ADB$ is the angle on the line $ADC$ next to $\angle BDC$, or use the angle sum in $\triangle ABD$: $\angle ADB = 180^\circ - 44^\circ - 24^\circ = 112^\circ$.

The largest angle of $\triangle ABD$ is $\angle ADB = 112^\circ$, so the longest side is the one opposite it: $AB$.

questions.solution_md: Base angles $68^\circ$; the second isosceles triangle $BDC$ gives $\angle DBC = 44^\circ$; then $\angle ABD = 24^\circ$ and $\angle ADB = 112^\circ$, the largest angle, so $AB$ is the longest side of $\triangle ABD$.

marking_scheme.step: (c) longest side AB, opposite the largest angle

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle B = (5x - 12)^\circ$ and $\angle C = (3x + 14)^\circ$, and $AB = AC$.

(a) Find $x$ and the angles $\angle B$ and $\angle C$.

(b) Find $\angle A$.

(c) Prove, for any triangle, that if two angles are equal then the sides opposite them are equal.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $AB = AC$, so $\angle B = \angle C$: $5x - 12 = 3x + 14 \Rightarrow 2x = 26 \Rightarrow x = 13$. Then $\angle B = 5 \times 13 - 12 = 53^\circ$ and $\angle C = 3 \times 13 + 14 = 53^\circ$.

**(b)** $\angle A = 180 - 53 - 53 = 74^\circ$.

**(c)** Let $\angle B = \angle C$ in $\triangle ABC$. Draw $AD \perp BC$ meeting $BC$ at $D$.

In $\triangle ADB$ and $\triangle ADC$: $\angle B = \angle C$, $\angle ADB = \angle ADC = 90^\circ$ and $AD = AD$ (common). So $\triangle ADB \cong \triangle ADC$ by AAS and $AB = AC$ (CPCT).

questions.solution_md: Equal sides give equal base angles, $x = 13$, so $\angle B = \angle C = 53^\circ$ and $\angle A = 74^\circ$. The converse is proved with the perpendicular $AD$ and AAS.

marking_scheme.step: (c) equal angles, right angles and common side AD
(c) AAS and AB = AC by CPCT

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle PQR$, $\angle P = (2x + 5)^\circ$, $\angle Q = (3x + 5)^\circ$ and $\angle R = (x + 20)^\circ$.

(a) Find $x$ and the three angles.

(b) Arrange the sides $PQ$, $QR$, $RP$ in ascending order of length and give the reason.

(c) A student draws this triangle with $PQ = 6$ cm, $QR = 8$ cm and $PR = 15$ cm. Is that possible? Give two checks.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Angle sum: $(2x + 5) + (3x + 5) + (x + 20) = 180 \Rightarrow 6x + 30 = 180 \Rightarrow x = 25$. So $\angle P = 2 \times 25 + 5 = 55^\circ$, $\angle Q = 3 \times 25 + 5 = 80^\circ$ and $\angle R = 25 + 20 = 45^\circ$.

**(b)** $\angle R < \angle P < \angle Q$ ($45^\circ < 55^\circ < 80^\circ$). The greater angle is opposite the greater side, so $PQ$ (opposite $R$) $< QR$ (opposite $P$) $< PR$ (opposite $Q$).

**(c)** *Order check:* $PR = 15$ cm is the longest, which agrees with $\angle Q$ being the largest, and $PQ = 6 < QR = 8$ agrees too. *Triangle inequality:* $PQ + QR = 6 + 8 = 14$ cm, which is less than $PR = 15$ cm. So no triangle exists with these sides: it is **not possible**; the order check alone is not enough.

questions.solution_md: $x = 25$ gives $55^\circ$, $80^\circ$, $45^\circ$; the sides in ascending order are $PQ < QR < PR$. The lengths $6$, $8$, $15$ have the right order but $6 + 8 = 14 < 15$, so they cannot form a triangle.

marking_scheme.step: (b) angles in order: R < P < Q
(b) sides PQ < QR < PR with the reason
(c) order of 6, 8, 15 agrees with the angles

questions.stem_md:
A water tank stands at a point $P$, $30$ m from a straight canal $l$. $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $l$. Points $A$ and $B$ of the canal lie on the same side of $M$, with $MA = 16$ m and $MB = 40$ m, so that $PA = 34$ m and $PB = 50$ m.

(a) Which of $PM$, $PA$, $PB$ is the shortest? Give the reason.

(b) Show, using angles, that $PB > PA$.

(c) A worker has a pipe of length $28$ m and another of length $31$ m. Can either of them join $P$ to a point of the canal? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $PM = 30$ m is the shortest. $PM$ is the perpendicular from $P$ to $l$, and the perpendicular is the shortest segment from a point to a line ($30 < 34 < 50$).

**(b)** $A$ lies between $M$ and $B$. $\angle PAB$ is an exterior angle of the right-angled $\triangle PMA$, so $\angle PAB > 90^\circ$ and it is larger than $\angle PBA$.

In $\triangle PAB$ the greater angle is opposite the greater side, so $PB > PA$: $50 > 34$.

**(c)** Every segment from $P$ to the canal is at least $PM = 30$ m. A pipe of $28$ m is shorter than $30$ m, so it **cannot** reach the canal.

A pipe of $31$ m is longer than $30$ m, so it can reach the canal, in fact at two points, one on each side of $M$ and at equal distances from $M$ (the two slanting segments make congruent right-angled triangles with $PM$ by RHS).

questions.solution_md: The perpendicular is shortest, $PM = 30$ m. The obtuse angle at $A$ makes $PB > PA$. A pipe shorter than the perpendicular ($28 < 30$) cannot reach the canal; one of $31$ m can, at two symmetric points.

marking_scheme.step: (a) PM is the shortest, as it is the perpendicular
(b) angle PAB is exterior to triangle PMA, so obtuse
(b) greater angle opposite greater side: PB > PA
(c) every segment is at least 30 m, so 28 m cannot reach
(c) 31 m can reach, at two symmetric points

questions.stem_md:
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = AC$. The point $E$ is on $AC$ and $F$ is on $AB$ with $AE = AF$. The segments $BE$ and $CF$ are drawn.

(a) Name the triangles to prove congruent and state the three equal parts with reasons.

(b) Prove that $BE = CF$ and that $\angle ABE = \angle ACF$.

(c) If $\angle A = 40^\circ$ and $\angle ABE = 22^\circ$, find $\angle ACF$, $\angle AEB$, $\angle BEC$ and $\angle EBC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle ACF$: $AB = AC$ (given), $\angle BAE = \angle CAF$ (the same angle $A$) and $AE = AF$ (given).

**(b)** The included angle is common, so $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle ACF$ by SAS. By CPCT, $BE = CF$ and $\angle ABE = \angle ACF$.

**(c)** $\angle ACF = \angle ABE = 22^\circ$ (part (b)). In $\triangle ABE$: $\angle AEB = 180^\circ - 40^\circ - 22^\circ = 118^\circ$.

$\angle BEC$ is on the line $AEC$: $\angle BEC = 180^\circ - 118^\circ = 62^\circ$. Also $\angle ABC = \dfrac{180^\circ - 40^\circ}{2} = 70^\circ$ (isosceles), so $\angle EBC = 70^\circ - 22^\circ = 48^\circ$.

questions.solution_md: SAS gives $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle ACF$, so $BE = CF$ and $\angle ABE = \angle ACF$. With the numbers: $\angle ACF = 22^\circ$, $\angle AEB = 118^\circ$, $\angle BEC = 62^\circ$ and $\angle EBC = 48^\circ$.

marking_scheme.step: (a) AB = AC, angle A common, AE = AF
(b) BE = CF and angle ABE = angle ACF by CPCT
